sections.b: Psalm 119 (Greek 118) has 176 verses in 22 eight-line stanzas, one for each Hebrew letter. Almost every verse names God's teaching with one of eight words (law, decrees, orders, rules, commands, rulings, word, saying). After three verses of blessing that echo Psalm 1, it is one long prayer to God by a servant under pressure who clings to God's word and asks to be taught. It sits in Book V between the Hallel (Psalms 113–118) and the Songs of Ascents (Psalms 120–134), and with Psalms 1 and 19 it is one of the three torah psalms that many scholars think shaped the Psalter into a book for study as well as song.

common: Psalm 119 is the longest chapter in the Bible.
uncommon: Will Soll argued that Psalm 119 is a lament in the voice of the exiled King Jehoiachin.

sections.h: Psalm 119: eight lines for every letter
sections.b: Psalm 119 is the fullest alphabet poem in the Bible: all eight verses of each stanza begin with the same letter, 22 × 8 = 176 verses. Where few words begin with a letter the poet improvises: every waw verse begins with "and" (Psalm 119:41–48), and five tet verses begin with "good" (Psalm 119:65–72). The eight lines per stanza match the eight words the poem uses for God's teaching. In Jewish practice the stanzas are read by letter: mourners recite the stanzas that spell a dead person's name, then those that spell neshamah, "soul".

No passage in the Bible praises God's torah more. The speaker loves it (Psalm 119:97), finds it sweeter than honey (Psalm 119:103) and better than gold (Psalm 119:72, 127), and calls it freedom (Psalm 119:45) and delight (Psalm 119:92). He uses eight words for it: law, decrees, orders, rules, commands, rulings, word and saying. Torah here is broader than a list of rules: it is God's whole teaching, written and spoken, and the speaker keeps asking God himself to teach him ("teach me your rules", six times). Scholars debate how much of the five books of Moses the poet had in front of him; Jon Levenson argues that the psalm expects teaching from God directly as well as from the written law. Christians differ on what this law means for believers (see the card on Psalm 119).

common: Psalm 119 uses eight different words for God's law and repeats them through the whole poem.
uncommon: Some scholars think the torah of Psalm 119 includes teaching God gives the speaker directly, not only the written books of Moses.

sections.b: Two of Psalm 119's eight words are words for speech: davar, "word" (24 times), and 'imrah, "saying" (19 times), often a promise. God's saying gives life (Psalm 119:50), is a lamp for the next step (Psalm 119:105), is refined like silver (Psalm 119:140), and stands as firm as the heavens and the earth (Psalm 119:89–91). Its sum is truth (Psalm 119:160), a line echoed in Jesus' prayer "your word is truth" (John 17:17). Ambrose's long commentary on the psalm and Bonhoeffer's unfinished meditation on it (1939–1940) both read it as a school of listening to God's word.

sections.h: The law as wisdom in Psalm 119
sections.b: Psalm 119 joins law and wisdom. The commands make the speaker wiser than his enemies, his teachers and the elders (Psalm 119:98–100), as Deuteronomy 4:6 promised. The law is his "delight" (sha'ashu'im, Psalm 119:92), the word Lady Wisdom uses of herself before God (Proverbs 8:30–31). The opening question, how a young man keeps his path clean (Psalm 119:9), is a wisdom teacher's question. Later Jewish writers made the link explicit: Ben Sira says Wisdom is the law Moses commanded (Sirach 24:23).

sections.h: Praying at midnight, before dawn and seven times a day
sections.b: Psalm 119 maps a day of prayer: at midnight (Psalm 119:62), before dawn and before the night watches (Psalm 119:147–148), and "seven times in a day" (Psalm 119:164). The Talmud tells how David rose at midnight to study (Berakhot 3b). Benedict's Rule takes 119:164 and 119:62 as the warrant for the monks' seven day offices and night office (chapter 16), and spreads Psalm 119 itself across the short daytime hours (chapter 18). Orthodox Christians read it at the midnight office.

Two traditions use Psalm 119 for the dead. In Jewish practice, at a funeral, the unveiling of a gravestone or the anniversary of a death, mourners read the eight-verse stanzas whose letters spell the person's Hebrew name, and then the stanzas for the letters of neshamah, "soul". In the Orthodox burial service the psalm (Greek Psalm 118, "Blessed are the blameless") is read or sung in sections with refrains, and at the matins of Holy Saturday the Lamentations for Christ in the tomb are sung between its verses. Both uses treat the psalm's love of God's word and its last cry, "come looking for your servant" (Psalm 119:176), as fitting words over the dead.

Psalm 119 says three times that affliction taught the speaker: before he was brought low he wandered (Psalm 119:67), being brought low taught him God's rules (Psalm 119:71), and God was faithful in it (Psalm 119:75). Yet the same psalm complains of exhaustion and danger (Psalm 119:81–87) and does not tell other sufferers their pain is deserved. The rabbis' "sufferings of love" (Berakhot 5a) and the discipline of Hebrews 12:10–11 grow from verses like these.

sections.h: A lament inside a torah psalm
sections.b: Psalm 119 is often read as a hymn to the law, but most of it is complaint and petition. The kaf stanza (Psalm 119:81–88) is a lament in miniature: worn out with waiting, like a wineskin in the smoke, counting his days, hunted with lies, almost finished. The speaker's loyalty to God's word does not spare him trouble; it is what he clings to in it.

sections.h: Psalm 119 in the Greek and at Qumran
sections.b:
The Greek Psalter (Psalm 118) follows the Hebrew closely but often reads the same consonants another way: "milk" for "fat" (Psalm 119:70), "frost" for "smoke" (Psalm 119:83), "idle talk" for "pits" (Psalm 119:85). It also uses one word for two of the eight law words. Single manuscripts swap one law word for another: in Psalm 119:105 Codex Sinaiticus has "law" for "word", and in Psalm 119:151 "ways" for "commands", where Rahlfs' Greek text keeps "word" and "commands" with the Hebrew. At Psalm 119:139 Rahlfs' text borrows "zeal for your house" from Psalm 69:9.

The Great Psalms Scroll from Qumran (11QPs-a) preserves much of the psalm, placed after Psalm 132, and smaller scrolls from Caves 1, 4 and 5 hold parts of it; some may have contained Psalm 119 alone. As reported in an English presentation of the published scroll texts, the scroll makes the same kind of swaps: "loyal love" for "rules" at Psalm 119:83, "be gracious to me" for "give me life" at Psalm 119:107, "word" for "loyal love" at Psalm 119:159. At Psalm 119:37 it agrees with the Hebrew "in your way".
